A hand pump drawing water from a well. Draw the pump handle raised with the piston down, then the handle pushed down with water rising in the pipe, then the water flowing out the spout. After each drawing, say which valve is open and which is closed.

A transformer changing voltage. Draw the primary coil with alternating current flowing in, then the magnetic field in the iron core, then the secondary coil with a different number of turns producing a different voltage. After each drawing, compare the number of turns on each coil.

A bicycle drivetrain showing how pedaling moves the wheels. Draw the pedals and chainring at the front, then the chain connecting to the rear sprocket, then the rear wheel turning as the chain pulls. After each drawing, say which part transfers the force.

A catapult launching a projectile. Draw the arm pulled back with tension in the rope, then the arm releasing and swinging forward, then the projectile flying through the air. After each drawing, identify the energy stored and released at each stage.

A refrigerator cooling food. Draw the compressor compressing the refrigerant gas, then the condenser coils on the back releasing heat, then the evaporator coils inside absorbing heat and making the inside cold. After each drawing, say whether heat is absorbed or released.

A fuse protecting a circuit from overload. Draw the normal circuit with current flowing through the fuse wire, then too much current heating the wire until it melts, then the broken circuit with the fuse blown and the bulb off. After each drawing, explain why the fuse melted.

An arch bridge distributing weight. Draw the bridge with a flat road deck, then the arched supports underneath transferring force to the abutments, then a heavy truck driving across with the arch compressing. After each drawing, describe where the compression force goes.

A DC motor spinning. Draw the permanent magnets on the sides, then the coil of wire in the middle with current flowing through it, then the commutator switching the current direction as the coil rotates half a turn. After each drawing, state which direction the coil will rotate.

A flowchart showing how to decide what to wear based on weather. Draw the start node, then a diamond asking 'Is it raining?', then branches for 'yes' leading to 'take umbrella' and 'no' leading to 'check temperature', then a final decision node. After each drawing, explain what each shape represents in a flowchart.

A binary search finding a number in a sorted list. Draw the sorted list of numbers 1 through 15, then the first check at the middle value 8, then the second check splitting the remaining half, then the final check finding the target. After each drawing, say how many numbers remain to search.

A stack data structure being used. Draw an empty stack, then three items pushed one by one onto the top, then two items popped off in reverse order. After each drawing, say which item is at the top of the stack.

A queue at a ticket counter. Draw an empty queue, then three people joining the queue one after another, then the first person being served and leaving from the front. After each drawing, say who is at the front of the queue.

A sorting algorithm arranging numbers. Draw five random numbers in a line, then the first pass comparing and swapping adjacent numbers, then the second pass with the largest number at the end, then the fully sorted list. After each drawing, say how many comparisons were made.

A binary tree being built. Draw the first node as the root with value 50, then a smaller value 30 inserted to the left, then a larger value 70 inserted to the right, then two more values 20 and 40 added. After each drawing, say whether each new value goes left or right.

A network connecting four computers. Draw the first computer, then a second connected by a cable, then a third connected through a switch, then all four connected in a mesh. After each drawing, say how many paths exist between any two computers.

A recursive function calling itself. Draw the first function call at the top, then it calling itself with a smaller input, then another call with an even smaller input, then the base case returning and each call returning upward. After each drawing, say how many calls are active.

A database index speeding up a search. Draw a table of unsorted names, then a sorted index list next to it pointing to the rows, then the search jumping to the middle of the index instead of scanning the whole table. After each drawing, compare the number of steps needed.

A hash table storing values by key. Draw an empty array of ten slots, then a key-value pair being hashed to slot 3, then another pair hashing to slot 7, then a collision where two keys hash to the same slot with a chain. After each drawing, explain how the hash function determines the slot.

A linked list of three nodes. Draw the first node containing the value 'A' and an arrow pointing to the next node, then the second node with 'B' pointing to the third, then the third node with 'C' pointing to null. After each drawing, show how to insert a new node 'D' between B and C.

An if-else decision structure in code. Draw a flowchart with a diamond asking 'Is the number positive?', then a branch for yes leading to 'print positive', a branch for no leading to another diamond 'Is it zero?', then final outputs. After each drawing, trace the path for the input -5.

A for loop iterating through an array. Draw an array of five numbers, then a variable i starting at 0 pointing to the first element, then i moving to 1 pointing to the second, then i reaching 4 pointing to the last. After each drawing, say which element is being accessed.

A graph with nodes and edges. Draw three nodes A, B, C with edges A-B and B-C, then add a fourth node D connected to A and C, then find the shortest path from A to C. After each drawing, count how many edges are in the shortest path.

A cache storing recently used data. Draw a CPU requesting data from main memory, then the data being stored in a small fast cache, then the CPU requesting the same data again and finding it in the cache. After each drawing, compare the speed of cache versus main memory.

A TCP handshake establishing a connection. Draw computer A sending a SYN to computer B, then B sending back SYN-ACK, then A sending ACK to confirm, then data flowing between them. After each drawing, say what state each computer is in.

A deadlock between two processes. Draw process 1 holding resource A and requesting resource B, then process 2 holding resource B and requesting resource A, then both processes stuck waiting. After each drawing, explain why neither can proceed.

A page table translating virtual to physical addresses. Draw a program using virtual address 0x100, then the page table mapping it to physical frame 5, then the CPU accessing physical address 0x500. After each drawing, show which part of the address is the page number and which is the offset.

A decision tree classifying animals. Draw the root asking 'Does it have fur?', then a branch for yes leading to 'Does it bark?', then a branch for no leading to 'Does it have feathers?', then the final leaf nodes with animal names. After each drawing, trace the path for a cat.

A client-server request cycle. Draw the client browser typing a URL, then the request traveling to the server, then the server processing and sending back a webpage, then the browser rendering the page. After each drawing, say what protocol is used at each step.

A bar chart showing the number of books read by four students. Draw the axes with student names on the bottom and number of books on the side, then a bar for Alice at 5 books, then a bar for Bob at 8 books, then bars for Carol at 3 and David at 6. After each drawing, say which student read the most and which read the least.

A line graph tracking temperature over a week. Draw the axes with days on the bottom and temperature on the side, then Monday at 20 degrees, then Tuesday at 22, then Wednesday at 25, then the rest of the week with a peak on Friday at 30. After each drawing, describe the trend.

A pie chart showing how a student spends their 24-hour day. Draw the full circle, then a slice for sleep at 8 hours, then a slice for school at 6 hours, then slices for homework, play, and meals dividing the rest. After each drawing, estimate what fraction of the day is spent sleeping.

A scatter plot showing the relationship between height and shoe size. Draw the axes with height on the bottom and shoe size on the side, then plot five points showing taller people generally having larger shoes, then add a trend line through the points. After each drawing, describe the correlation.

A histogram showing the distribution of test scores. Draw the axes with score ranges on the bottom and number of students on the side, then bars showing most scores clustered between 70 and 90, with a few low scores around 50 and a few high scores around 100. After each drawing, describe the shape of the distribution.

A box plot comparing two classes on a math test. Draw the number line, then a box for class A with the median at 75 and the range from 60 to 90, then a box for class B with the median at 85 and the range from 70 to 95. After each drawing, compare the medians and spread.

A probability tree showing coin flips. Draw the first branch splitting into heads and tails, then from each branch two more branches for the second flip, then the four possible outcomes listed at the ends. After each drawing, calculate the probability of getting two heads in a row.

A bell curve showing the normal distribution of adult heights. Draw the axes with height on the bottom and frequency on the side, then the symmetric bell shape centered at 170 cm, then mark one standard deviation above and below the mean. After each drawing, estimate what percentage falls within one standard deviation.

A stacked bar chart showing sales of three products over four quarters. Draw the first quarter with bars for product A, B, C stacked on top of each other, then the second quarter with all three growing, then the third and fourth quarters showing trends. After each drawing, identify which product sold the most overall.

A Venn diagram showing the overlap between students who play soccer, basketball, and both. Draw two overlapping circles, label the left circle 'Soccer' with 8 students, the right circle 'Basketball' with 6 students, and the overlapping area with 3 students who play both. After each drawing, calculate how many students play at least one sport.

A frequency table showing the number of pets per family. Draw a table with columns for 'Number of Pets' and 'Number of Families', then fill in rows: 0 pets for 5 families, 1 pet for 12 families, 2 pets for 8 families, 3 pets for 3 families. After each drawing, calculate the average number of pets.

A double bar chart comparing rainfall in two cities across six months. Draw the axes with months on the bottom, then pairs of bars for each month, City A in blue and City B in red, with City A getting more rain in winter and City B in spring. After each drawing, compare the seasonal patterns.

A cumulative frequency graph showing exam scores. Draw the axes with score on the bottom and cumulative count on the side, then a curve rising slowly at first, then steeply through the middle scores, then leveling off at the top. After each drawing, estimate the median score from the graph.

A sample space diagram for rolling two dice. Draw a 6 by 6 grid with the first die on the rows and the second die on the columns, then shade all the cells where the sum is 7, then count how many ways to roll a sum of 7. After each drawing, calculate the probability of rolling a sum of 7.

A stem and leaf plot showing test scores. Draw the stem column with tens digits 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, then leaves showing individual scores: 5|2 means 52, 6|578 means 65, 67, 68, etc. After each drawing, find the mode and median from the plot.

A misleading graph with a truncated y-axis. Draw a bar chart where the y-axis starts at 80 instead of 0, making a small difference between two bars look huge, then redraw the same data with the y-axis starting at 0 to show the true difference. After each drawing, explain how the truncated axis changes the visual impression.

A moving average smoothing a noisy stock price chart. Draw a jagged line going up and down for daily prices, then a smooth curve following the general trend calculated as a 7-day moving average. After each drawing, compare the smoothness of the two lines.

A tree diagram showing the probability of drawing marbles from a bag. Draw a bag with 3 red and 2 blue marbles, then the first draw splitting into red (3/5) and blue (2/5), then from each branch the second draw with adjusted probabilities. After each drawing, calculate the probability of drawing two red marbles in a row.

A heat map showing temperature across a country. Draw a grid map with cities in rows and months in columns, then color the cells from blue for cold to red for hot, with northern cities blue in winter and southern cities red all year. After each drawing, describe the temperature gradient from north to south.

A triangle transforming through three types. Draw an equilateral triangle with all sides equal, then an isosceles triangle with two equal sides, then a scalene triangle with all sides different. After each drawing, label the equal sides and state the type.

A circle with its key parts labeled. Draw the circle with center point O, then a radius from O to the edge, then a diameter passing through O, then a chord not passing through the center. After each drawing, name the part that was just added.

A right triangle being used to explain the Pythagorean theorem. Draw a right triangle with legs of 3 and 4 units, then squares built on each side, then the square on the hypotenuse with area 25 equal to the sum of the squares on the legs. After each drawing, verify that 3 squared plus 4 squared equals 5 squared.

A quadrilateral family tree. Draw a square with all sides equal and all angles 90 degrees, then a rectangle with opposite sides equal, then a rhombus with all sides equal but angles not 90, then a parallelogram with opposite sides parallel. After each drawing, compare the properties.

A rotation of a shape by 90 degrees. Draw an L-shaped figure in the first quadrant, then rotate it 90 degrees clockwise around the origin, then rotate it another 90 degrees. After each drawing, describe where the shape has moved relative to the axes.

A reflection of a triangle across a line. Draw a triangle on the left side of a vertical mirror line, then the reflected triangle on the right side at the same distance from the line, then both triangles with the mirror line between them. After each drawing, compare the distances from the mirror line.

A translation of a shape by a vector. Draw a house shape at position (1,1), then an arrow showing the translation vector (3,2), then the same house shape at the new position (4,3). After each drawing, describe how the shape moved along the grid.

A tessellation of regular hexagons. Draw a single hexagon, then a second hexagon sharing one side with the first, then a third filling the gap, then a honeycomb pattern of many hexagons covering the surface. After each drawing, count how many hexagons meet at each vertex.

A net of a cube unfolding. Draw a closed cube in 3D perspective, then the cube unfolding into a cross-shaped net of six squares, then the flat net with all faces labeled. After each drawing, identify which face is opposite which.

A cylinder showing its volume. Draw a cylinder with height and radius labeled, then the circular base with the formula for area, then the cylinder filled with unit cubes to show height times base area. After each drawing, calculate the volume given the dimensions.

A pair of similar triangles. Draw a small triangle with sides 2, 3, 4, then a larger triangle with sides 4, 6, 8 that is a scaled copy, then the two triangles overlaid showing corresponding angles are equal. After each drawing, state the scale factor.

A tangent to a circle. Draw a circle with center O, then a point P on the circumference, then a line through P that touches the circle at exactly one point, then the radius OP drawn perpendicular to the tangent line. After each drawing, describe the angle between the radius and the tangent.

An angle changing from acute to obtuse. Draw an acute angle of 30 degrees, then a right angle of 90 degrees, then an obtuse angle of 120 degrees, then a straight angle of 180 degrees. After each drawing, classify the angle as acute, right, obtuse, or straight.

A 3D rectangular prism shown from three views. Draw the front view showing a rectangle, then the side view showing a different rectangle, then the top view showing the length and width. After each drawing, identify which dimension is visible in that view.

A dilation of a shape from a center point. Draw a small square near a center point C, then rays from C through each vertex of the square, then a larger square at the points where the rays extend twice as far. After each drawing, compare the side lengths of the two squares.

Parallel lines cut by a transversal. Draw two horizontal parallel lines, then a diagonal line crossing both, then label the alternate interior angles as equal, then the corresponding angles as equal. After each drawing, identify which angles are equal.

A cone with its dimensions labeled. Draw the cone with a circular base, then the height from the apex to the center of the base, then the slant height from the apex to the edge of the base. After each drawing, explain how the slant height relates to the height and radius using the Pythagorean theorem.

A regular pentagon with its lines of symmetry. Draw a regular pentagon, then one line of symmetry from a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side, then all five lines of symmetry intersecting at the center. After each drawing, count how many lines of symmetry a pentagon has.

A scale drawing of a room. Draw a bedroom floor plan with a scale of 1 cm to 1 meter, then a bed measuring 2 cm by 1.5 cm representing a 2 m by 1.5 m bed, then a desk and chair drawn to the same scale. After each drawing, calculate the actual dimensions from the scale measurements.

A sphere showing great circles. Draw a sphere as a circle with shading, then a great circle around the equator, then another great circle through the poles, then the equator and the polar circle intersecting at right angles. After each drawing, explain why these are called great circles.

A family budget being planned for the month. Draw a table with income at the top, then rent, food, utilities, and savings as expense categories, then a pie chart showing what percentage goes to each category. After each drawing, explain which category takes the largest share.

A supply and demand graph showing the price of apples. Draw the axes with price on the vertical and quantity on the horizontal, then a downward-sloping demand curve, then an upward-sloping supply curve, then the intersection point marking the equilibrium price. After each drawing, describe what happens at the equilibrium point.

A bank account growing with compound interest. Draw a piggy bank with 100 dollars, then after one year with 105 dollars at 5 percent interest, then after two years with 110.25 dollars, then after five years with 127.63 dollars. After each drawing, calculate how much interest was earned that year.

A classroom showing different social roles. Draw a teacher at the front teaching, then students at their desks listening, then a group of students working together on a project, then one student helping another understand a problem. After each drawing, describe the social interaction happening.

A trade between two countries. Draw Country A with lots of wheat and Country B with lots of steel, then a ship carrying wheat from A to B, then a ship carrying steel from B to A, then both countries with more of both goods after trade. After each drawing, explain why both countries benefit from trade.

A population pyramid showing age distribution. Draw the axes with age groups on the vertical and population on the horizontal, then a pyramid shape with a wide base for a young population, then a narrow base for an aging population, then a column-like shape for a stable population. After each drawing, describe what each shape implies about birth rates.

A community garden project bringing neighbors together. Draw an empty lot with weeds, then neighbors meeting to plan the garden, then volunteers planting vegetables and flowers, then the finished garden with people harvesting and talking. After each drawing, describe the social benefits of the shared space.

A stock market chart showing a company's share price over a year. Draw the axes with months on the bottom and price on the side, then the price rising steadily for six months, then a sudden drop on news of a recall, then a gradual recovery over the next three months. After each drawing, explain what caused the price change.

A voting ballot being counted in an election. Draw a ballot box with people casting votes, then the ballots being sorted into piles for each candidate, then a bar chart showing the final vote counts, then the winner being announced. After each drawing, calculate what percentage of the vote the winner received.

A family tree showing three generations. Draw a grandfather and grandmother at the top, then their two children in the middle with their spouses, then four grandchildren at the bottom. After each drawing, identify the relationships between the people.

An insurance policy protecting a house. Draw a house with a family inside, then a storm damaging the roof, then the insurance company paying for the repairs, then the house restored with a new roof. After each drawing, explain how insurance spreads the risk among many people.

A carbon tax reducing pollution. Draw a factory emitting smoke, then the government placing a tax on each ton of carbon emitted, then the factory installing cleaner technology to avoid the tax, then the air becoming cleaner. After each drawing, explain how the tax changes behavior.

A minimum wage increase affecting workers. Draw a worker earning minimum wage counting their money, then the government raising the minimum wage, then the worker earning more and spending more at local shops, then the shop hiring an extra employee due to increased demand. After each drawing, trace the economic ripple effect.

A public library providing free resources to the community. Draw a library building with books inside, then a child borrowing a book for free, then a student using a computer to do research, then a job seeker printing a resume. After each drawing, list the resources that are free to the public.

A budget deficit and surplus visualized. Draw a government with money coming in as taxes and going out as spending, then the spending exceeding income creating a deficit shown in red, then the income exceeding spending creating a surplus shown in green. After each drawing, explain how the government can reduce a deficit.

A neighborhood watch program reducing crime. Draw a street with no one watching and a theft occurring, then neighbors forming a watch group, then the group patrolling and reporting suspicious activity, then the crime rate dropping. After each drawing, explain how community involvement improves safety.

A currency exchange rate changing over time. Draw a sign showing 1 dollar equals 0.85 euros, then a month later 1 dollar equals 0.75 euros, then a traveler exchanging dollars getting fewer euros, then a graph of the exchange rate over six months. After each drawing, say whether the dollar strengthened or weakened.

A progressive tax system explained. Draw three people earning different incomes: 30,000, 60,000, and 120,000 dollars, then show the tax rate increasing with income, then calculate the tax each person pays, then show the after-tax income. After each drawing, explain why higher earners pay a higher percentage.

A cultural festival celebrating diversity. Draw people from different backgrounds each bringing a traditional dish, then music and dance performances from different cultures, then children learning about other traditions through crafts, then the whole community eating together. After each drawing, describe one cultural tradition shown.

A central bank adjusting interest rates. Draw the economy growing too fast with high inflation, then the central bank raising interest rates, then businesses and consumers borrowing less, then inflation slowing down. After each drawing, explain how higher interest rates reduce spending.
